NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Scaling Latent Reasoning via Looped Language Models
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Modern LLMs are trained to "think" primarily via explicit text generation, such as chain-of-thought (CoT), which defers reasoning to post-training and under-leverages pre-training data. We present and open-source Ouro, named after the recursive Ouroboros, a family of pre-trained Looped Language Models (LoopLM) that instead build reasoning into the pre-training phase through (i) iterative computation in latent space, (ii) an entropy-regularized objective for learned depth allocation, and (iii) scaling to 7.7T tokens. Ouro 1.4B and 2.6B models enjoy superior performance that match the results of up to 12B SOTA LLMs across a wide range of benchmarks. Through controlled experiments, we show this advantage stems not from increased knowledge capacity, but from superior knowledge manipulation capabilities. We also show that LoopLM yields reasoning traces more aligned with final outputs than explicit CoT. We hope our results show the potential of LoopLM as a novel scaling direction in the reasoning era. Our model is available here: http://ouro-llm.github.io.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Learning Ordinal Probabilistic Reward from Preferences
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Reward models are crucial for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values and intentions. Existing approaches follow either Generative (GRMs) or Discriminative (DRMs) paradigms, yet both suffer from limitations: GRMs typically demand costly point-wise supervision, while DRMs produce uncalibrated relative scores that lack probabilistic interpretation. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel reward modeling paradigm: Probabilistic Reward Model (PRM). Instead of modeling reward as a deterministic scalar, our approach treats it as a random variable, learning a full probability distribution for the quality of each response. To make this paradigm practical, we present its closed-form, discrete realization: the Ordinal Probabilistic Reward Model (OPRM), which discretizes the quality score into a finite set of ordinal ratings. Building on OPRM, we propose a data-efficient training strategy called Region Flooding Tuning (RgFT). It enables rewards to better reflect absolute text quality by incorporating quality-level annotations, which guide the model to concentrate the probability mass within corresponding rating sub-regions. Experiments on various reward model benchmarks show that our method improves accuracy by $\textbf{2.9%}\sim\textbf{7.4%}$ compared to prior reward models, demonstrating strong performance and data efficiency. Analysis of the score distribution provides evidence that our method captures not only relative rankings but also absolute quality.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: The Mathematical Collective Unconscious: Jungian Archetypes within the Latent Space
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Carl Jung theorised that the human psyche contains an inherited framework, the collective unconscious, populated by universal archetypes. As large language models (LLMs) are trained on vast corpora of textual data, this paper investigates whether they spontaneously construct distinct archetype-like regions within their high-dimensional latent spaces. The paper proposes that these regions function as spatial constraints that naturally organise semantically related narratives. To evaluate this, we applied cosine similarity and angular distance metrics across thirteen experiments utilising OpenAIs text-embedding-3-small model. The paper contains two experimental sections the first section explores these ideas using synthetically constructed narratives, the results of which act as a baselines for experiments conducted in the second section where the synthetic data is replaced by human-authored literature (Shmoop corpus), unedited dream reports (DreamBank corpus), and culturally distilled folklore (Andrew Langs Fairy Books). The results show that archetypal roles occupy distinct, measurable regions in the latent space. Crucially, these regions remain compact and consistent because of narrative structure rather than simple word overlap. Additionally, text category dictates spatial distribution: dream reports concentrate within Trickster and Shadow regions, while traditional folklore distributes evenly across all tested archetypes. We conclude that transformer latent spaces encode stable regions which appear to correspond to recognised Jungian archetypes.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: A Counterfactual Graph Approach to Oppositional Narrative Analysis
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Distinguishing legitimate critical speech from coordinated conspiracy narratives is a pressing challenge for the integrity of the online information ecosystem, yet prevailing approaches rely on labeled entity roles and rigid predefined schemas that fail to capture the diffuse and context-dependent nature of participation in such narratives. We propose a modular framework that extracts an entity-interaction graph directly from narratives and reasons over it for classification, without depending on annotated node-level labels. Our pipeline enumerates candidate entity spans from a domain-adapted BERT encoder and learns a bipartite graph structure, which is then classified with a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer. To make predictions interpretable, we cast the graph as a hypergraph and apply a counterfactual distillation procedure that estimates the Individual Treatment Effect of each node, pruning extraneous entities to recover a minimal predictive subgraph. On the standard PAN Oppositional Narratives benchmark, our model achieves a macro F1-score of 0.93 and an MCC of 0.84, reaching state-of-the-art performance with roughly one-third of the parameters of the next best system, while pruning the graphs by 75.2% on average without altering predictions. Our results demonstrate that graph-based representations coupled with counterfactual inference offer both strong predictive accuracy and transparency into the entities driving conspiratorial discourse.
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.comment: 14 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: Trustworthy AI for Good (AI4GOOD)

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: In-Place Indic Tokenizer Expansion and Continual Pretraining of Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: We adapted Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B for eight Indian languages without changing its backbone architecture. We expanded the vocabulary in place from 131,072 to 163,072 entries using continued byte-pair encoding and AdaptMix rebalancing, reducing tokens per word by 38.6%. We initialized new input and output rows by averaging their original constituent rows, then trained them on 90% Indic and 10% English text before updating the backbone. Continual pretraining then progressed through broad training, high-quality annealing, and long-context training over approximately 1.27 trillion tokens. The annealed checkpoint gained 12.9 points on the Indic MILU benchmark but lost 3.4 on English MMLU. We also report practical negative results. Direct token addition underperformed continued byte-pair encoding. AdamW weight decay changed rows intended to stay fixed. Perplexity on an Indic-heavy holdout did not select the learning rate that best preserved English performance.

Information Retrieval (Top Venues & Labs.title: Understanding ChatGPT Citations: Evidence from Production Web Search Across Model Generations
Information Retrieval (Top Venues & Labs.summary: Generative engines such as ChatGPT Web retrieve webpages to answer user queries, but only a subset are shown as citations. Understanding this retrieval-to-citation process is important for generative engine optimization (GEO), which aims to improve content visibility in generative-engine responses. However, prior studies mainly analyze final responses, leaving the internal execution process and its variation across model settings less understood. To this end, we conduct an observational study of four ChatGPT Web settings from ChatGPT 5.2 to 5.5, covering Instant and Thinking modes at the URL, hostname, and entity levels. We examine how ChatGPT rewrites queries, retrieves candidate webpages, and selects references. The Instant settings remain mostly single-round, while GPT-5.4 Thinking frequently performs multiple retrieval rounds. Across repeated runs, candidates retrieved more often are also more likely to be cited. We then evaluate Google Search and the OpenAI Responses API as external proxies. Responses API candidates provide broader coverage, while its citations more closely match sources cited by ChatGPT Web. Both proxies match ChatGPT Web better at the hostname and entity levels than at the exact-URL level. Even when combined, they recover only about one quarter of cited URLs. We further test whether these external signals remain predictive when combined. Within the external candidate set, a supervised model combining them reaches AUCs above 0.74 for GPT-5.3 and GPT-5.5 at all three levels. These findings suggest that GEO should distinguish retrieval visibility from citation visibility, account for rewritten queries and run-to-run variation, and consider hostname- and entity-level presence in addition to exact URLs. Differences across settings also suggest that GEO strategies should be re-evaluated when the deployed setting or serving environment changes.

Multiagent Systems (Top Venues & Labs).title: PopGen: Generating Semantically Diverse Populations for Zero-Shot Coordination
Multiagent Systems (Top Venues & Labs).summary: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, exposing a cooperator to partners with diverse strategies during training is key to better collaboration at test time. However, existing methods typically rely on trajectory-level proxies to measure diversity, which may label two distinct trajectories of the same strategy as diverse. Instead, our key insight is to leverage LLMs' ability to describe behaviorally distinct agents in environments, similar to how humans can recognize high-level strategies. To this end, we introduce PopGen, a framework that synthesizes semantically diverse agents from scratch using LLMs. PopGen first generates a diverse set of textual descriptions of agent behaviors, then translates each behavior into a code policy that can be executed within the environment. We show that cooperators trained against PopGen populations achieve robust zero-shot cooperation with unseen partners, outperforming population-play baselines across four collaborative environments. We further show that semantic diversity scales with PopGen population size, improving the cooperator's worst-case performance, and we identify design choices that preserve population quality while maximizing diversity. Our code is available at https://github.com/labicon/PopGen.

Databases (Core).title: Join Order Enumeration and Optimization for Double-Star and Helix Join Graphs
Databases (Core).summary: Join ordering is classic problem in data management. We highlight the connection between structure-specific dynamic programming algorithms and the mathematical enumeration of the possible merge trees from a join graph. We present two case studies, on double-star and helix shaped join graphs, that we believe carry useful techniques for a toolbox of building structure-specific join optimizers. For the double-star case, we show how the enumeration leads directly to a significantly improved search algorithm, whereas for the helix case we show that a algorithm derived from the mathematical enumeration is not necessarily better than structure-agnostic algorithms.

Databases (Core).title: Recall-Bounded Staleness for Filtered Multi-Tenant ANN Graph Indexes under Concurrent Updates
Databases (Core).summary: Production vector search must continuously ingest, delete, and re-tenant vectors while serving low-latency, high-recall, metadata-filtered approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) queries for many tenants with per-tenant service-level objectives. Existing graph-based ANN systems address these requirements largely in isolation, leaving recall during concurrent re-optimization without an analytical bound. We develop a graph-based index that combines streaming updates, filtered search, and multi-tenancy, with one theoretical result and two system mechanisms. Our theory decomposes per-tenant recall loss into staleness from updates not yet integrated into the graph and filtered navigability determined by the local density of points satisfying a tenant's predicate. The staleness component exhibits anti-amortization on a merge-based graph, integrating a larger batch of inserts increases recall degradation super-linearly, so larger merges do not reduce total staleness loss. Holding the insert horizon fixed while increasing merge size 20x, we observe a monotonic decrease in terminal recall@10 from 99.44% to 99.01%. For filtered search, the theory gives a parameter-free frontier-mass relationship in local predicate density and a query-averaged per-tenant recall bound. We instantiate the bound with a filter and tenant-aware staging cache and a select-not-resize scheduler with per-tenant staleness ceilings. On a FreshDiskANN substrate, the ceiling eliminates tight-tier SLA violations under the evaluated churn workload, while merge reordering changes terminal recall by only 0.02 percentage points. The results show how recall bounds can guide background maintenance without relying on merge resizing as a recall control mechanism.

Databases (Core).title: Use Of Convolutional Neural Networks In Detection Of Branch Dieback Disease In Pequi Trees
Databases (Core).summary: This study aims to evaluate and compare convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, specifically AlexNet, Inception, LeNet, VGG16, and MobileNet, for diagnosing branch dieback (seca-dos-ponteiros) in pequi trees (Caryocar brasiliense). This disease represents a severe threat to tree development and fruit yield, causing substantial economic and ecological losses. The methodology implements computer vision techniques using Python libraries, including Scikit-learn, NumPy, TensorFlow, and Matplotlib, to process and evaluate visual data. The CNN models analyze images of leaves, branches, and flower spikes to detect pathological patterns, such as alterations in texture and coloration. Ultimately, this comparative analysis identifies the most effective architecture for accurately distinguishing healthy plants from diseased ones.

Databases (Core).title: Efficient K-generalizable Learned Search
Databases (Core).summary:
Learned top-K search improves the accuracy-latency trade-off of graph-based vector search, but existing methods target a fixed K. Serving real-world workloads with various K values thus incurs preprocessing cost proportional to the number of distinct Ks.
  We present OMEGA, which supports efficient arbitrary K learned search with the preprocessing cost of one top-1 model. It achieves so by reducing learned top-K search to repeated masked learned top-1 search with refinement, using carefully crafted trajectory features that generalize across Ks. OMEGA further employs rank-wise confidence allocation to tame error accumulation during refinements and applies a statistical forecast method to reduce model invocation overhead without compromising recall. Across nine dataset-scale configurations, OMEGA meets the 0.95 recall target and reduces mean latency by up to 65% (average: 23%; median: 20%) compared with learned search methods (including LAET, DARTH, MultiK-DARTH, ANNiE, and Ada-ef) at their lowest-preprocessing configurations. On production traces, it reduces total CPU time by up to 28% versus traditional HNSW search.

Databases (Core).title: DBA-Bench: A Production-Fidelity Benchmark for LLM-Based Database Operations Agents
Databases (Core).summary: LLM-based database agents show promise, but differences in task scope, testbeds, and success criteria hinder direct comparison. A shared benchmark must also preserve the operational conditions that determine whether diagnosis and remediation succeed in practice. We present DBA-Bench, guided by operational realism, outcome-first evaluation, and controlled scenario reproducibility. It evaluates agents in live PostgreSQL and distributed TiDB deployments with active workloads, stateful behavior, and multi-source observations. Success requires satisfying scenario-specific operational objectives without violating safety constraints. The primary evaluation covers 231 bounded scenarios across five operational domains, while 10 persistent scenarios extend evaluation to continued operation across interacting events. We evaluate eight automated baselines, including four frontier foundation models, two open-weight models, and two GPT-5.5-backed database agents. Our evaluation exposes gaps between diagnosis, effective remediation, and safe execution across both database systems. Agents can identify root causes yet fail to restore operational objectives. Even when objectives are restored, the executed actions can violate safety constraints. Persistent scenarios expose a gap between clearing individual blockers and sustaining business service: agents leave competing workloads uncoordinated and previously completed repairs unchecked after subsequent changes.

Databases (Core).title: LYNX: Analytical Program Synthesis via Grounding and Closed-Loop Refinement
Databases (Core).summary: LLM-powered data analytics aims to translate natural language instructions into executable analytical programs over underlying data. However, existing approaches, whether treating LLMs as intent-to-code translators or as standalone analytical engines, often fail to reliably align domain semantics with complex schemas and heterogeneous metadata, resulting in brittle execution and semantically inconsistent analytical outputs in real-world workloads. We present LYNX, a multi-agent framework that formulates LLM-driven analytics as a schema- and knowledge-constrained analysis problem rather than a single-pass generation task. LYNX organizes analytical synthesis into a closed-loop workflow of planning, generation, verification, and refinement through three role-specialized agents that collaboratively enforce schema grounding, semantic consistency, and execution correctness. To address domain ambiguity and schema misalignment, LYNX integrates Semantic-Structural Distillation and Stage-Aware Allocation (SSD-SAA). A delta-guided iterative revision continuously diagnoses and repairs semantic and execution-level failures, substantially improving synthesis robustness. We evaluate LYNX on two NL-to-SQL benchmarks, BIRD-SQL Mini-Dev and the more challenging Spider 2.0-Lite. Experimental results demonstrate strong performance and efficiency, achieving 10.66% to 59.54% execution accuracy across lightweight and commercial models, while reducing token consumption by 70.53% compared with the prior most efficient method. Our framework displays high generalization over different backbones, from open-source, lightweight models to the latest commercial models. Additional case studies on quantitative finance analytics and complex multi-relational SQL workloads further demonstrate the framework's robustness, scalability, and practical applicability in real-world analytical scenarios.

Databases (Core).title: A BUD You Can Count On: Efficient, Verifiable Membership Proofs
Databases (Core).summary: A block typically changes only a small fraction of blockchain state, yet producing a state root makes validators update an authenticated tree spanning it all. We show how to support verifiable reads from the writes alone. We introduce Block Update Digests (BUDs), that commit to a block's writes and link each key touched in that block to its previous modification. An optional prior-value record lets one successor BUD authenticate the value between modifications, replacing the baseline's two BUD openings. SuperBUDs summarize those writes over longer intervals, letting a reader verify that a value remained unchanged without checking every intervening block. Thanks to BUDs and SuperBUDs, validators can just keep ordinary flat state while still serving proofs of current and historical values, including deletion. We prove soundness and completeness for reads at or after a key's first logged modification when the required proof data is available. In experiments with the baseline format, a 50x increase in state size raises the measured base-BUD cost by just 1.24x. In paired QMDB experiments, lowering its garbage-collection activation threshold raises process CPU time by 1.3-2.7x and device bytes written by 1.6-2.4x relative to its dormant configuration. BUD authentication requires no corresponding relocation of live entries. In the evaluated baseline, two-digest read-layer payloads stay below 800 bytes, and warm hash-path verification takes at most 146 μs at p99. Authenticated reads need not make validators maintain an authenticated tree over the entire state.

Databases (Core).title: TurboProm: Low Cost and High Performance Metrics Observability at Scale
Databases (Core).summary:
Many large enterprise and cloud deployments rely on metrics observability solutions (e.g., Prometheus) to monitor key performance indicators of system health (e.g., CPU, memory, network, app-level statistics). Monitoring and analyzing these metrics presents a significant challenge in terms of cost-latency tradeoffs at scale. Ideally, system operators would like immediately deployable and backwards compatible solutions to improve the cost-latency tradeoffs without significant impact on the fidelity of their observability applications. Unfortunately, existing solutions including state-of-art timeseries databases and custom approximate querying solutions fail on one or more aspects.
  In this paper, we present the design and implementation of TurboProm, a backwards-compatible drop-in accelerator for metrics observability deployments. TurboProm recasts metrics analytics tasks using a semantic-preserving summary view rather than classical query-centric view. Instead of estimating query results on raw timeseries metrics data, TurboProm uses semantic-preserving summaries that enable high-fidelity analytics with significant cost-latency improvements. We present a practical implementation of TurboProm that can be retrofitted to any existing observability deployment. We evaluate TurboProm on diverse real and synthetic workloads against state-of-art solutions and show that it can provide significant reduction in query latency and cost. Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Compute-Optimal Scaling Laws for Spiking Language Models
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Spiking neural networks target energy-efficient language modeling through sparse, binary activations, but the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff of spiking language models is uncharacterized at scale. Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: When Dynamic Scaling Fails: A Scale-State Feedback Governs Recurrent-State Quantization in Linear-Attention and SSM LLMs
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Linear-attention and state-space LLMs carry long context in a fixed-size recurrent state, and quantizing that state is the natural way to cut its cost during long decode. Unlike a weight tensor, the state is rewritten at every step, so a quantizer applied at each step sits inside the recurrence and its errors compound. INT4 that leaves synthetic recall perfectly intact at the start destroys it a thousand steps later. The mechanism is a feedback between the quantizer scale and the state it is derived from. Yoking that scale to a full-precision reference removes the resulting norm explosion entirely, yet recovers only 1.8 of the 5.4 nats lost, so numerical instability and functional degradation are separable failures. The remainder is a resolution problem that locating outliers does not solve, since every outlier-aware scheme here loses to plain persistent scaling. Allocating bits across layers does help, but under article-disjoint splits a learned allocation collapses onto the trivial rule of protecting the first few layers. Run out to 32K, group-wise INT4 is worth no more than discarding the state. Contain the scale rather than locate outliers, and report the decode horizon at which a bit-width was certified.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: RELAGRAM: Recursive Latent Graph Model for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Latent recursion repeatedly processes internal representations through the same neural network. Recent work has shown this approach to be effective on structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku and maze solving. However, whether latent recursion can support neural routing remains unclear. RELAGRAM encodes a capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) instance as edge tokens; a compact transformer recurrently updates the latent representations of these tokens. On CVRP-100 instances, the 0.53M-parameter RELAGRAM achieves gaps to a PyVRP reference of 13.4%, 9.8%, and 8.3% under greedy decoding, eightfold symmetry augmentation, and 256-candidate search, respectively. Trained only on CVRP-100, RELAGRAM generalizes zero-shot to CVRP-500 and CVRP-1000, achieving gaps of 15.6% and 21.7% under 256-candidate search. Together, these results demonstrate that latent recursion is a promising approach to neural routing.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Toward a Multimodal Foundation Model for Plasma State Reconstruction
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Plasma experiments observe coupled physical states through sparse, heterogeneous, and incomplete diagnostics. Using 250 synthetic VPIC simulations at fixed reference electron beta $β_{e0}=0.2$, with 225 training runs and 25 disjoint validation runs, we train a 5.5M-parameter residual 3D U-Net to reconstruct three magnetic-field components and electron density from incomplete observations. The model combines spatial-only pooling, which preserves all 24 temporal frames, with global spatiotemporal self-attention and rotary positional encoding. Independently masking magnetic and density modalities across random, grid, block, and temporal patterns enables sparse sensing, cross-modal completion, density super-resolution, and temporal completion with a single set of weights and no task-specific retraining. With density fully hidden, just 0.1% magnetic spatial visibility reduces median density NRMSE from approximately 0.9 to 0.1. Conversely, observed density improves current-density reconstruction when magnetic data are absent or extremely sparse. With no magnetic observations, roughly 1% density visibility approaches the density reconstruction accuracy achieved with fully observed magnetic fields, although current structure remains more dependent on direct magnetic measurements. Full magnetic conditioning also stabilizes completion of missing future density frames. These results demonstrate bidirectional cross-modal predictive coupling within this simulation regime. Generalization across plasma regimes or to experimental measurements remains untested.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: SEEK: Agentic Knowledge Graph Retrieval for Secure Code Generation
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate functionally correct code while introducing exploitable security weaknesses, particularly when developers specify functionality without explicit security requirements. Recent state-of-the-art approaches mitigate this problem using external security knowledge, but largely rely on flat similarity-based retrieval over independent artifacts, making it difficult to infer the relevant vulnerability space and retrieve targeted knowledge when direct matches are unavailable. We propose SEEK, an agentic Graph RAG framework for secure code generation that constructs a security knowledge graph using the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) taxonomy as its structural backbone and injects it with curated real-world CVE vulnerability-fix instances. At inference time, a Planner Agent predicts potential CWE weaknesses associated with the developer query, which guide Graph Scoping to restrict retrieval to relevant regions of the CWE taxonomy before deterministic multi-faceted candidate ranking. A Selection Agent subsequently validates the predicted weaknesses and retrieved candidates prior to code generation. Across five open-source LLMs, we evaluate SEEK in an out-of-distribution setting on CodeGuard+ and CyberSecEval, spanning C, C++, and Python. SEEK achieves the highest SecurePass@1 of 77.45% on CodeGuard+ and the highest aggregate ICD pass rate of 79.45% on CyberSecEval, surpassing prior approaches. Moreover, SEEK achieves 85.2% SecurePass@1 across 13 unseen CWE types with no directly linked vulnerability-fix instances, demonstrating strong generalizability, while maintaining acceptable inference latency costs.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Pro-t-VAE: Closed-Form Student's t Mixtures for Robust Prototype Discovery
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: We present a robust deep generative framework for unsupervised image prototype discovery, built on a heavy-tailed Student's t mixture prior, that bridges statistical robustness and mathematical tractability. Existing generative approaches typically rely on noise-prone Gaussian priors or computationally intensive diffusion models; neither simultaneously provides explicit latent structure nor exact analytic optimization. While diffusion models can yield strong priors, iterative sampling and intractable likelihoods limit scalability and interpretability for prototype discovery. We address these issues by constructing a Student's t latent space via a Bayesian scale-mixture formulation. This yields a fully closed-form augmented ELBO for unsupervised Student's t mixture variational autoencoders, which, to our knowledge, is the first such objective applied to robust image prototype discovery, avoiding biased variational approximations and high computational costs in prior heavy-tailed or diffusion-based frameworks. Treating precision as a latent variable automatically modulates each data point's influence, downweighting outliers to learn a data-dependent measure of trust. The result is improved robustness, accuracy, and efficiency, with well-separated latent representations and more stable manifold learning than state-of-the-art methods. We validate our model on standard vision benchmarks and challenging neuroimaging tasks. In brain MRI-driven neurodegenerative disease analysis, our model recovers clean, anatomically coherent prototypes where clinical noise often collapses rare subtypes. These results highlight the ability of our framework to preserve anatomy-associated patterns for precise discovery in clinical settings. Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Refining Compositional Diffusion for Reliable Long-Horizon Planning
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Compositional diffusion planning generates long-horizon trajectories by stitching together overlapping short-horizon segments through score composition. However, when local plan distributions are multimodal, existing compositional methods suffer from mode-averaging, where averaging incompatible local modes leads to plans that are neither locally feasible nor globally coherent. We propose Refining Compositional Diffusion (RCD), a training-free guidance method that steers compositional sampling toward high-density, globally coherent plans. RCD leverages the self-reconstruction error of a pretrained diffusion model as a proxy for the log-density of composed plans, combined with an overlap consistency term that enforces consistency at segment boundaries. We show that the combined guidance concentrates sampling on high-density plans that mitigate mode-averaging. Experiments on challenging long-horizon tasks from OGBench, including locomotion, object manipulation, and pixel-based observations, demonstrate that RCD consistently outperforms existing methods.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Efficient K-generalizable Learned Search
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary:
Learned top-K search improves the accuracy-latency trade-off of graph-based vector search, but existing methods target a fixed K. Serving real-world workloads with various K values thus incurs preprocessing cost proportional to the number of distinct Ks.
  We present OMEGA, which supports efficient arbitrary K learned search with the preprocessing cost of one top-1 model. It achieves so by reducing learned top-K search to repeated masked learned top-1 search with refinement, using carefully crafted trajectory features that generalize across Ks. OMEGA further employs rank-wise confidence allocation to tame error accumulation during refinements and applies a statistical forecast method to reduce model invocation overhead without compromising recall. Across nine dataset-scale configurations, OMEGA meets the 0.95 recall target and reduces mean latency by up to 65% (average: 23%; median: 20%) compared with learned search methods (including LAET, DARTH, MultiK-DARTH, ANNiE, and Ada-ef) at their lowest-preprocessing configurations. On production traces, it reduces total CPU time by up to 28% versus traditional HNSW search.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Random Fourier Features in Near-Linear Time
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Random Fourier features approximate a shift-invariant kernel in $\mathbb{R}^d$, such as the Gaussian kernel $\exp(-\tfrac12\|x-y\|_2^2)$, using independent samples from its spectral measure to construct an unbiased estimator for the kernel value with subgaussian concentration. However, generating $m$ such features requires $O(md)$ time. A long line of work on structured random features has accelerated this computation for the Gaussian kernel and other radial kernels, albeit with weaker concentration guarantees. We close this gap by showing a random feature map that can be computed in near-linear time $O((d+m)\log d)$ and yields near-subgaussian concentration. We obtain it through a new and tighter analysis of the Fastfood feature map of Le, Sarlós and Smola (ICML 2013), using Brascamp-Lieb inequalities and the Schoenberg representation of radial kernels.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: VitaBench: Memory Lifecycles Beyond Retrieval
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Long-term memory benchmarks for language agents primarily evaluate whether information from earlier interactions can be retrieved and used when relevant. Persistent memory systems face an additional problem before future use is known: deciding whether a memory should remain exact, be compressed, consolidated, or deleted. Existing benchmarks capture long-range retrieval, temporal reasoning, evidence reuse, and incremental interaction, but do not directly evaluate these earlier representation decisions. We formalize memory lifecycle evaluation and introduce VitaBench, a benchmark that makes lifecycle decisions measurable through repeated memory reviews and full-horizon counterfactual evaluation. VitaBench contains a controlled Diagnostic tier that isolates future-use patterns and a Naturalistic tier that composes them into generated customer-service-style interaction streams. We characterize lifecycle decision structure with three diagnostics: lifecycle headroom, measuring the advantage of adaptive choices over the best fixed strategy; horizon reversal, measuring when short-horizon decisions change under delayed consequences; and optimal-action diversity, measuring whether different memory states favor different lifecycle operations. Across both tiers, VitaBench exhibits substantial lifecycle structure: lifecycle headroom is 1.364 in Diagnostic and 1.405 in Naturalistic, and 60.2% and 56.5% of states, respectively, change their preferred action between short and full horizons. A learned delayed lifecycle policy further improves over the best fixed strategy on VitaBench-Naturalistic, reaching 101.5 versus 83.4 joint utility. These results show that retrieving past information and deciding how it should persist are distinct evaluation problems, and that lifecycle management requires evaluation of the delayed consequences of representation decisions.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Accelerating Cross-Model LLM Inference via Attention Map Reuse
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: LLM-augmented data workflows often involve multiple heterogeneous models operating over substantial shared context, such as schemas, tool specifications, interaction history, and intermediate results. Although prefix caching can reduce prefilling overhead, existing approaches are largely limited to reuse within the same model because KV states are tightly coupled to model-specific architectures. We present MapFlow, a system for efficient heterogeneous LLM serving via cross-model attention map reuse. Instead of reusing KV states, MapFlow reuses attention maps, which capture token dependency patterns and are more transferable across models. To enable efficient and accurate reuse, we combine partial recomputation with lightweight linear translation across layers and heads. To make attention reuse practical for long contexts, we further introduce block-level sparse compression and a fused retrieval kernel. Experiments show that MapFlow reduces prefilling latency and improves end-to-end serving efficiency while preserving generation quality across heterogeneous model pairs and multi-turn routing workloads. These results suggest that attention maps provide an effective reusable state for heterogeneous LLM serving, especially in prefix-heavy data workflows. Our code is available: https://github.com/PKU-DAIR/MapFlow.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: TagBO: LLM-Driven Task-Aware Graph Bayesian Optimization for Scientific Discovery
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Mixed-variable optimization in scientific discovery often requires exploring large combinatorial spaces under costly experimental evaluations, making sample?efficient Bayesian optimization (BO) essential. However, existing BO methods typ?ically rely on structural descriptors to define similarity among categorical variables, implicitly assuming that structural similarity reflects similarity in task performance. In scientific optimization, this assumption is often violated, leading to surrogate representations that are poorly aligned with the optimization objective. To address this limitation, we propose TagBO (Task-aware Graph Bayesian Optimization), a method that integrates LLM-derived relational priors with descriptor-based struc?tural information for mixed-variable Bayesian optimization. Rather than directly using LLM outputs as predictive scores, TagBO treats LLM outputs as a potentially noisy source of task-aware relational priors and extracts coarse ordinal relational signals from LLM reasoning to construct task-aware similarity structures for scien?tific optimization. TagBO then performs constrained Gaussian process Bayesian optimization over the resulting joint discrete-continuous representation space. Ex?periments on diverse chemistry and materials formulation tasks demonstrate that TagBO consistently improves sample efficiency under fixed evaluation budgets across LLMs of varying capabilities.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: How Much Can Repeated Running Buy? A Measured Variance Ceiling for LLM Code Evaluation
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: A benchmark score is a measurement whose uncertainty has two sources: an aleatoric component from stochastic decoding and an epistemic component from the finite problem set. Using 16 models on 99 recent LeetCode-style problems with two prompts and five runs each (15,840 judged runs in a fully crossed design), we estimate both components and ask a design question: how much can repeated running buy? First, the pooled-binomial interval that repeated-run protocols invite answers neither question of interest---it is about $2\times$ too narrow for generalisation to new problems and $2\times$ too wide for the fixed problem set---and under correctly clustered intervals, 12 of 15 adjacent leaderboard pairs are statistically unresolved. Second, the variance ceiling $1+μ_w/σ_b^2$, the largest factor by which repetition can reduce score variance, has median 1.34 across models (range 1.05--1.71), so repetition can narrow confidence intervals by at most 23% on this benchmark, and by 14% for the median model. Third, once the cost of adding verified problems is priced in, the precision-optimal repeat count is $R^{*}=\sqrt{μ_w c_p/(σ_b^2 c_g)}$, and the variance curve is flat around it: on this benchmark the decisive reason to repeat is not precision but identification---two to three runs suffice to estimate the components that the ceiling and the fixed-benchmark interval require. All three are measurements of one benchmark at one decoding temperature, and we state explicitly what they do and do not license.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Router Sensitivity Under Lightweight Fine-Tuning Identifies Prunable Experts in Mixture-of-Experts Models

Recent theory shows that experts whose router weights change least during fine-tuning can be pruned with provable accuracy preservation, yet the guarantee assumes full fine-tuning. We show that the signal can be elicited through a brief parameter-efficient adaptation. We fine-tune with a lightweight adapter, rank experts by the induced router change, and prune the least-changed experts in one shot. On Mixtral-8$\times$7B-Instruct, router-only LoRA trains 0.002% of parameters and retains 27.54% MMLU-Pro accuracy with half the experts removed, against roughly 16% for magnitude and random pruning. Signal quality improves monotonically with adapter size, reaching 28.76%, and declines as adaptation spreads beyond the router. Under their shared budget, IA3 reaches 28.04% while Houlsby reaches 25.39%. The criterion transfers to Qwen1.5-MoE fine-tuned for mathematical reasoning, retaining 49.7% mean accuracy over eleven benchmarks with half the experts removed. Structural pruning reduces memory by 49% and per-token latency by 37%. Lightweight router sensitivity therefore makes provably motivated, task-conditioned expert pruning practical at scale.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: PGSB: Pretrained-Guided Shared Basis for LoRA Model Merging
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Large pretrained models have achieved remarkable success across diverse domains, yet adapting them to multiple downstream tasks remains challenging: full fine-tuning is costly, while maintaining separate task-specific models is storage-inefficient and fails to produce a unified multi-task model. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) offers an efficient alternative for Model Merging by representing each task adaptation as a low-rank update over frozen pretrained weights. However, existing LoRA merging methods often treat task-specific updates as directly comparable objects and merge them in their original low-rank parameter spaces. This overlooks two key factors: which update directions provide reliable shared support across tasks, and how these directions should be re-parameterized with respect to the pretrained weights before merging. To address this limitation, we propose Pretrained-Guided Shared Basis (PGSB), a two-stage framework for LoRA model merging. PGSB first identifies shared directions among task-specific LoRA updates, and then re-parameterizes these directions using their interaction with the pretrained weights, producing a more suitable basis for merging. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PGSB consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across multiple benchmarks. Codes are available at https://github.com/Kitschnada/Pretrained-Basis .

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: When Attention Does Not Explain the Peak: Temporal Reference vs. Forecast Output in Attention-Based Time-Series Forecasting
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Attention maps are often interpreted as evidence of what a forecasting model uses when making predictions. In our load-forecasting model, a CLS representation of historical demand queries 24 future exogenous horizon tokens through cross-attention, inviting a temporal interpretation in which highly attended horizons may appear to explain forecast peak timing. We test this interpretation using a horizon-level attention descriptor, $Ψ_{\mathrm{out}}$. Across 31 day-aligned windows of the Panama load dataset, the forecast achieves a median peak-time error of 0 h and a 51.6% exact-match rate, whereas the argmax of $Ψ_{\mathrm{out}}$ has a median error of 5 h and 0% exact match. The forecast peak is closer to the observed peak in 27 of 31 windows. This dissociation is not merely an argmax artifact: within $\pm1$ h, attention reaches only $1.16\times$, $1.11\times$, and $1.14\times$ the uniform baseline around observed, predicted, and weekly-naive peaks, respectively, indicating weak and non-selective concentration. Yet the attention profile is structured, with cross-window consistency of 0.83. Replacing 12 future weather features with their training-set means makes the profile nearly uniform, showing sensitivity to future weather variation rather than fixed horizon position alone. The dissociation is also reproduced across three random-seed runs. These results show that structured, input-sensitive, and reproducible horizon-level cross-attention need not provide a valid peak-selective explanation of forecast behavior. The observed behavior is instead consistent with an internal horizon-reference role for integrating future exogenous information, although this functional role is not causally established.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: DEFT: Disentanglement-Enhanced Fine-Tuning for EEG Foundation Models
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: EEG foundation models (EFMs) have improved EEG representation learning by transferring knowledge from large-scale multi-subject pretraining to downstream tasks. DEFT encourages branch disentanglement of pretrained tokens into task-oriented content and subject-consistent style, then performs downstream prediction from the content branch. It instantiates this factorize-before-classify design with recursive Gaussian refinement, temporal-variance regularization, subject-aware contrastive learning, and reconstruction. Experiments across multiple EEG datasets and four EFM backbones show that DEFT improves matched fine-tuning baselines. Further ablations and analyses support the intended content/style branch organization.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Scaling Laws for Multimodal Data Mixtures
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Frontier AI systems are increasingly natively multimodal, jointly pretrained on multiple modalities, such as text, vision, and audio. However, the scientific understanding of the multimodal data mixtures used to pretrain these systems --- how much of each modality to mix, and at what potential interference cost to the others --- is largely absent or gatekept. In this work, we derive data mixing scaling laws for three modalities: text, vision, and audio. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly adopt Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, as MoEs scale efficiently and partially limit cross-modal interference. We therefore use MoEs to conduct 268 experiments ranging from 457M to 8.3B parameters, on up to 150 billion tokens. Our work leads to multiple actionable insights into multimodal data mixing for training MLLMs. First, compute optima are modality-specific: audio modality is model-heavy, favoring scaling parameters over tokens, while text and vision require balanced scaling of model size and data. Second, repeating vision or audio data beyond 2x yields negligible benefits. Finally, cross-modal interactions are highly asymmetric: vision strongly interferes with audio, whereas audio's interference with learning text and vision is negligible. Overall, we provide a principled foundation for understanding the multimodal data mixtures needed to train frontier MLLMs.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: PyINE: A Framework for Scalable Elicitation and Oversight via Code Execution
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Reasoning models can remain capable of solving a task while still defaulting to cheaper but misleading shortcuts. This creates a central oversight problem: when a model gives an answer with plausible but incomplete reasoning, can an overseer determine whether that output should be trusted? To study this problem, we introduce PyINE, a framework for scalable elicitation and oversight using instrumented Python programs as a verifiable execution substrate. In PyINE, programs define task environments, execution traces provide authoritative labels for outcomes and intermediate facts, and task variants can be generated mechanically rather than through static human annotation. We instantiate the framework in PyINE-v1, a first release built from nearly one million deterministic execution traces and over 500,000 matched LLM-generated code variants used for counterfactual evaluation. Using standard RL with verifiable rewards on cue-varied tasks, we train a shortcut-following model that improves substantially at predicting execution outcomes while still making systematic errors when misleading human-facing cues conflict with the program's realized behavior. We then evaluate activation probes, trained text classifiers, prompted judges, and a lightweight debate protocol as overseers of this model. We find that performance pooled at the dataset level can hide weak coverage of the failures that matter most: cheap learned overseers often miss rare shortcut-driven errors, while stronger model-based checks are more balanced but substantially costlier and harder to turn into reliable thresholded decisions. PyINE-v1 turns this failure-mode coverage problem into a reusable experimental setting for developing oversight methods that are verifiable, failure-mode-aware, and cost-sensitive.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: PotentialEP: Backprop-Free Training of CIFAR-Scale Generative Models via Equilibrium Propagation
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Generating an image with a diffusion or flow-matching model typically involves integrating a velocity field for hundreds of sequential steps. That computation suits a GPU poorly and an analog neuromorphic substrate well, where one fast, low-power physical relaxation could replace the whole sequence. Two things are needed: a generative algorithm whose computation is a relaxation, and a way to train it without backpropagation, whose global gradient transport is hard to realise in analog. Energy Matching supplies the first, sampling by gradient-descent relaxation on a time-independent potential - but obtaining the gradient that descent follows is itself a backward pass, once per integration step. We prove that a predictive coding network with a single linear injection term added to its energy relaxes to a state whose visible layer carries that gradient inherently, with an error that vanishes for small injection strengths. An Energy Matching model trained by backpropagation can therefore be loaded into this network unchanged and sampled by relaxation alone, matching the original model's FID to within 0.04 at CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32 scale. The network can also be trained without backpropagation: Equilibrium Propagation reproduces backpropagation's parameter updates to a cosine similarity of 0.9998, and training end to end with those updates reaches an FID of 3.64 on unconditional CIFAR-10 against 3.54 for backpropagation. To our knowledge this is the first CIFAR-10 generative model trained with Equilibrium Propagation, and the first at competitive quality by any backpropagation-free rule. This quality does not require group normalisation or attention: an architecture of only convolutions and pointwise nonlinearities, both native to an analog crossbar, reaches an FID of 3.51 when trained by backpropagation.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce PANINI-DR, a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate PANINI-DR on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven state-of-the-art deep-research harnesses, all using a shared language-model backbone and frozen corpora. PANINI-DR achieves the strongest average performance across the three benchmarks. On BrowseComp-Plus, it achieves 73.3% accuracy, outperforming the next-best harness by 16.0 points. Its advantage is strongest on hard questions, where it answers nearly twice as many as the next-best harness. Ablations further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does checking each finding against its cited evidence before it is reused. Because a model can answer correctly from memory alone, we also analyze the evidence retained by each harness. PANINI-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how harnesses compare and further strengthens PANINI-DR's advantage.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Exploring Jailbreak Vulnerability Across Depth-Based Dynamic Inference in Large Language Models
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been shown to be computationally expensive and vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, in which adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment and induce harmful responses. To address this inefficiency, a range of techniques have been proposed to enable efficient LLM inference. Depth-based dynamic inference has demonstrated promising results by enabling outputs to be generated from intermediate layers. It offers the flexibility to adjust model behavior based on the available resource budget. However, how this flexibility affects the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap via a comprehensive investigation into the impact of depth-based dynamic inference on the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Specifically, we make the following key observations: 1) Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreak attacks than deeper ones; 2) Exit depth affects how easily the adversarial suffix can be optimized, with deeper exits reaching lower attack loss; and 3) Adversarial suffixes affect utility uniformly across exit depths. These insights can help design dynamic inference methodologies that are more robust to jailbreak attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/LassNajmuldeen/balcony-jailbreaking

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Compute-Optimal Scaling Laws for Spiking Language Models
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Spiking neural networks target energy-efficient language modeling through sparse, binary activations, but the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff of spiking language models is uncharacterized at scale. We present the first Chinchilla-style IsoFLOP scaling study of a spiking language model, sweeping SpikeGPT-family models (RWKV backbone) from width 384 to 1536 across compute budgets from $3\times10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ FLOPs on FineWeb-EDU. We report two findings. First, the compute-optimal frontier is $N_{opt} \propto C^{0.56}$, close to the 0.50 that Hoffmann et al. report for dense Transformers, so spiking does not change how parameters and data should be traded off under a compute budget. Second, against non-spiking RWKV and Transformer baselines trained the same way, the loss gap splits into a backbone cost of about 0.16 nats that does not change with compute and a spiking cost that falls from 0.34 to about 0.23 nats and then levels off. These results give the first compute-optimal recipe for spiking language models and quantify the accuracy cost of their sparsity.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: RegExtract: A Benchmark for PFAS Regulatory Information Extraction with LLMs
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Extracting structured information from regulatory documents is a critical but challenging task. Relevant facts are scattered across long, legally dense texts, and traceability of extracted facts to their source is essential for verification. With increasing awareness of the environmental and health impacts of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), regulatory documents have expanded significantly, varying in scope and product relevance, making interpretation challenging for manufacturers and policymakers. We introduce RegExtract, a benchmark for structured information extraction from PFAS regulatory documents, comprising 488 human-annotated field instances across 20 US state documents and 46 regulations. Each field instance includes a value and a provenance entry, yielding 976 entries in total. We define a typed, multi-field schema targeting key elements such as material definitions, permitted uses, and product exemptions, and propose provenance-aware evaluation metrics tailored to regulatory text. Through experiments with open- and closed-source LLMs across prompting strategies, document condensing methods, and schema partitioning approaches, we find that document identification fields remain challenging, and that field-specific few-shot examples improve extraction. This work lays the groundwork for AI tools for hazardous substance identification, question answering, and compliance monitoring. The code and data are available at https://github.com/IBM/PFAS-regulations.
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.comment: Accepted to the AI for Law Workshop at ICML 2026, Seoul, South Korea

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Tracing Agentic Failure from the Flow of Success
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Failure attribution for LLM-based agentic systems, i.e., identifying which steps in a failure trajectory caused the task to fail, is critical for debugging and improving these systems. Existing approaches either rely on prompting-based pipelines, which are computationally expensive, or require post-training on failure trajectories with step-level error annotations, which are costly to collect and difficult to scale. We argue that a practical failure attribution model should be lightweight and trainable without step-level supervision on failure data. To this end, we address unsupervised failure attribution, i.e., training exclusively on successful trajectories and identifying error steps at inference time given a failure trajectory. We propose OAT, which casts this problem as one-class learning with neural controlled differential equations, modeling the dynamical pattern of successful trajectories in latent space. At inference time, each step in a failure trajectory is assigned an anomaly score based on its deviation from the dynamics learned on successful trajectories, which is then used to form a set of error steps. With training on only 100 successful trajectories, experiments show that OAT is 200--5000 $\times$ faster than prompting-based baselines, and, at the same time, consistently outperforms them in both in-domain and out-of-distribution datasets with +20% and +7% F1 scores, respectively, demonstrating that OAT is a promising and efficient direction for diagnosing agentic system failures.
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: XL-SafetyBench: A Country-Grounded Cross-Cultural Benchmark for LLM Safety and Cultural Sensitivity
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Current LLM safety benchmarks are predominantly English-centric and often rely on translation, failing to capture country-specific harms. Moreover, they rarely evaluate a model's ability to detect culturally embedded sensitivities as distinct from universal harms. We introduce XL-SafetyBench, a suite of 5,500 test cases across 10 country-language pairs, comprising a Jailbreak Benchmark of country-grounded adversarial prompts and a Cultural Benchmark where local sensitivities are embedded within innocuous requests. Each item is constructed via a multi-stage pipeline that combines LLM-assisted discovery, automated validation gates, and dual independent native-speaker annotators per country. We report Attack Success Rate (ASR) alongside Neutral-Safe Rate (NSR) to separate principled refusal from non-engagement, and introduce the Cultural Sensitivity Rate (CSR) for recognizing embedded sensitivities. Evaluating 10 frontier and 27 local LLMs reveals two key findings. First, strong jailbreak robustness does not always come with strong cultural awareness, showing why the two should be evaluated separately. Second, local models exhibit a strong ASR-NSR trade-off (r = -0.81), suggesting that low attack success in several local models reflects non-engagement rather than safe refusal. XL-SafetyBench enables more nuanced, cross-cultural safety evaluation in the multilingual era.
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.comment: NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations & Datasets Track

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Scaling Laws for Multimodal Data Mixtures
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Frontier AI systems are increasingly natively multimodal, jointly pretrained on multiple modalities, such as text, vision, and audio. However, the scientific understanding of the multimodal data mixtures used to pretrain these systems --- how much of each modality to mix, and at what potential interference cost to the others --- is largely absent or gatekept. In this work, we derive data mixing scaling laws for three modalities: text, vision, and audio. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly adopt Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, as MoEs scale efficiently and partially limit cross-modal interference. We therefore use MoEs to conduct 268 experiments ranging from 457M to 8.3B parameters, on up to 150 billion tokens. Our work leads to multiple actionable insights into multimodal data mixing for training MLLMs. First, compute optima are modality-specific: audio modality is model-heavy, favoring scaling parameters over tokens, while text and vision require balanced scaling of model size and data. Second, repeating vision or audio data beyond 2x yields negligible benefits. Finally, cross-modal interactions are highly asymmetric: vision strongly interferes with audio, whereas audio's interference with learning text and vision is negligible. Overall, we provide a principled foundation for understanding the multimodal data mixtures needed to train frontier MLLMs.

Information Retrieval (Top Venues & Labs.title: PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces
Information Retrieval (Top Venues & Labs.summary: Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce PANINI-DR, a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate PANINI-DR on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven state-of-the-art deep-research harnesses, all using a shared language-model backbone and frozen corpora. PANINI-DR achieves the strongest average performance across the three benchmarks. On BrowseComp-Plus, it achieves 73.3% accuracy, outperforming the next-best harness by 16.0 points. Its advantage is strongest on hard questions, where it answers nearly twice as many as the next-best harness. Ablations further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does checking each finding against its cited evidence before it is reused. Because a model can answer correctly from memory alone, we also analyze the evidence retained by each harness. PANINI-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how harnesses compare and further strengthens PANINI-DR's advantage.

Information Retrieval (Top Venues & Labs.title: Efficient K-generalizable Learned Search
Information Retrieval (Top Venues & Labs.summary:
Learned top-K search improves the accuracy-latency trade-off of graph-based vector search, but existing methods target a fixed K. Serving real-world workloads with various K values thus incurs preprocessing cost proportional to the number of distinct Ks.
  We present OMEGA, which supports efficient arbitrary K learned search with the preprocessing cost of one top-1 model. It achieves so by reducing learned top-K search to repeated masked learned top-1 search with refinement, using carefully crafted trajectory features that generalize across Ks. OMEGA further employs rank-wise confidence allocation to tame error accumulation during refinements and applies a statistical forecast method to reduce model invocation overhead without compromising recall. Across nine dataset-scale configurations, OMEGA meets the 0.95 recall target and reduces mean latency by up to 65% (average: 23%; median: 20%) compared with learned search methods (including LAET, DARTH, MultiK-DARTH, ANNiE, and Ada-ef) at their lowest-preprocessing configurations. On production traces, it reduces total CPU time by up to 28% versus traditional HNSW search.

Information Retrieval (Top Venues & Labs.title: Co-adaptive Rule Routing and Constraining for Structured Knowledge Retrieval
Information Retrieval (Top Venues & Labs.summary: Structured knowledge retrieval acquires task-relevant evidence from structured knowledge sources for downstream tasks. Existing methods rely on unconstrained retrieval or predefined query-rule supervision, such as author-paper rules for scientific discovery and anatomy-drug rules for precision medicine. Such supervision is rarely available in practice. We propose Co-Adaptive Rule Routing and Constraining Retrieval (CoRE), which jointly learns which reasoning rule to assign to each query and how to retrieve evidence under that rule, without predefined query-rule pairs. A routing agent selects a rule, and its corresponding retriever traverses the knowledge base and ranks evidence that satisfies the rule's constraints. Because routing and retrieval are interdependent, CoRE alternates between reinforcement learning for the routing policy and contrastive learning for the rule-constrained retriever. The selected rules provide supervision for retriever training, while retrieval performance rewards the routing policy. This closed-loop process enables both components to co-adapt without explicit query-rule supervision. Experiments on STaRK-QA datasets across scientific discovery, biomedical reasoning, and e-commerce knowledge management demonstrate CoRE's effectiveness. Ablations show the benefit of co-adapting the router and retriever. Generation-based routing transfers across datasets and benefits from multi-domain pretraining followed by target-specific fine-tuning. Analysis of rule usage across queries also informs automatic rule refinement and discovery.

Multiagent Systems (Top Venues & Labs).title: Iterate on an LLM, Serve on an SLM
Multiagent Systems (Top Venues & Labs).summary: As frontier LLMs gain more capabilities, the cost to run them also goes up. At the same time, small language models (SLMs) also gain more capabilities but have largely been able to keep their cost stable, offering 5-40 times cheaper inference for the narrow, repetitive subtasks that agents decompose work into. However, the standing limiting factor is getting the correct behavior out of a small model in a fast, efficient, and economical way. Unfortunately, in most cases, zero-shot small models fail narrow production tasks. Furthermore, retraining one every time the behavior changes is too slow to iterate on. We propose doing both in sequence. First, develop the desired behavior in prompt space, on a frontier model, with immediate feedback from live traffic. Then, once the behavior converges, distill the recorded production behavior (not synthetic imitations of it) into an SLM through supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We show a proper use case of this method through a scheduling agent for home-care agencies that fans out a single yes/no safety decision per caregiver-shift pair on GPT-5.4-nano. A LoRA-tuned Qwen3-8B trained on 11.6k recorded production decisions reaches 0.913 agreement, while the teacher (GPT-5.4-nano), re-run on its own recorded prompts, agrees with itself only 72.7% of the time, pointing to the fact that the SLM may also be more consistent. Furthermore, when the two disagreed, a blinded professional scheduler sided with the student 48-29. Finally, we find that the SLM has approximately 2.5 times lower median latency and is a fraction of the cost. We believe this lifecycle of quick building, live feedback, and cheap inference is a blueprint for others building similar systems.
