Multiagent Systems (Top Venues & Labs).title: Generalized Intention Modeling in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
Multiagent Systems (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Modeling an opponent's intent is critical for effective decision-making in non-cooperative, competitive, and general-sum multi-agent reinforcement learning. Existing opponent modeling methods encode intent using an embedding derived from episode information chosen a priori, such as the opponent's next action or a future environment state, and use this to guide the ego-agent's behavior. These approaches assume that the chosen information is universally representative of intent; however, we show empirically that this is not the case as intentions are often task- and environment-dependent. To address this, we introduce a task-adaptive opponent modeling framework that learns a performance-driven mixture of multiple intent representations. We further introduce a new intention representation that maximizes mutual information with the ego-agent's future returns, thereby capturing opponent information that is most directly relevant to performance. Our approach consistently matches or exceeds the performance of state-of-the-art baselines across diverse tasks and yields insights into when and why different opponent modeling strategies succeed.

Databases (Core).title: A GPU Engine for Sparse Matrix-Vector Products on $k^2$-Tree-Compressed Graphs
Databases (Core).summary: The $k^2$-tree is a compact representation of Boolean matrices: it stores the recursive hierarchy of their non-empty submatrices, with neither values nor coordinates, and serves rows and columns alike. Its traversal, however, locates the children of each node by rank queries, a chain of dependent irregular loads that leaves a GPU waiting on memory. We implement sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) on $k^2$-trees for the GPU. Since the traversal does not depend on the vector, the positions of the children are static: we descend the tree one level at a time and obtain them from a parallel prefix sum or from a sampled directory of about 0.1 bits per node. Descending in tiles bounds the temporary memory by the depth of the tree, so the device memory of a product is known before it runs. The same traversal computes right and left products, for one vector or a batch, over the plus-times, Boolean and tropical semirings. We evaluate the engine on an NVIDIA GB10 and an H100 with fourteen Wikidata, Software Heritage, web and social graphs of up to 1.2 billion edges, against cuSPARSE, a grammar-compressed GPU engine and a Boolean CSR. Our results show that the tree is 2.3-27x smaller than the CSR of cuSPARSE and that, with its last internal level cached, a product takes 0.7-2.4x the time of cuSPARSE on the right and 0.27-2.6x on the left. On a 1.2-billion-edge graph, a product needs 1.1 GB on the device, 9x less than cuSPARSE. The engine is memory bounded: the $k^2$-tree is the format of choice when device memory, not time, is the constraint.

Databases (Core).title: O2N2: Efficient Doubly Oblivious Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
Databases (Core).summary:
Privacy-preserving approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search allows clients to search from an untrusted server without revealing sensitive queries, and is useful in scenarios like medical diagnostics and credit scoring. Among the various privacy-preserving primitives, trusted execution environments (TEEs) have much lower overhead than heavy cryptographic ones, yet they leak memory access patterns, enabling adversaries to infer query contents.
  Oblivious RAM (ORAM) can be used to hide those access patterns at $\mathrm{O}(\log N)$ asymptotic cost, but existing high-performance ANN search algorithms (e.g., IVF or HNSW) exhibit complex, data-dependent access patterns that are unfriendly for ORAM. Furthermore, standard ORAM constructions typically assume there exists a small amount of trusted storage, which weakens the security guarantees and is not always feasible. Solutions that eliminate such trusted storage (known as {\em double obliviousness}) typically degrade performance further to $\mathrm{O}(\log^2 N)$.
  We introduce O2N2, a doubly oblivious ANN framework built around single-path search in randomly rotated $k$-d tree forests. A pointer-based Circuit ORAM stores the search structure, with separate storage for compact internal nodes and vector-bearing leaves. Each visited leaf is processed by an oblivious selection network, and fixed-schedule duplicate removal and selection combine the local results into the final top-$k$.
  We evaluate O2N2 on real-world datasets and further test its scalability on 100 million vectors. For 10-NN and 100-NN search at the specified high-recall targets, it achieves a $9.8$--$125.9\times$ speedup over the fastest doubly oblivious baselines.

Databases (Core).title: From FAIR to AI-FAIR Metadata-First Infrastructure for AI-Enabled Science
Databases (Core).summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and their capabilities have advanced rapidly over the past few years, leading to widespread interest and adoption in the biological and ecological sciences. However, the data infrastructure and computational resources that provide the foundation for AI workflows in ecology and biodiversity science remain fragmented. Moreover, the flow of value remains largely unidirectional: data move from collectors, through repositories and aggregators into models, and finally to research products or management actions. The derived value, such as corrected taxonomies, annotations, quality flags, and insights, rarely returns to source communities. We propose an extension of the original FAIR principles to address the needs of AI-ready infrastructure: the AI-FAIR metadata criteria, which place AI-enabled science in the context of a bidirectional Question-Data-Model triangle. This framework is designed to facilitate large-scale content-based analysis across diverse collections and ensure that the scientists generating the data benefit from the AI-enabled advances built on their data. Alongside these criteria, we introduce an agentic evaluation workflow that both rates existing datasets on the AI-FAIR and traditional FAIR criteria and provides actionable feedback where critical metadata is missing or incomplete. This modular dataset evaluation tool, paired with a domain-appropriate checklist, translates these principles into a reusable assessment of machine-learning readiness, AI-readiness for specified tasks, traceability, and ethical and CARE-aligned stewardship. Through this approach we aim to create a community-informed system to close the model data loop, so that AI also enriches data to further enable scientific discovery.
Databases (Core).comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, Code available at: https://github.com/FAIR4AI-Bio/evaluator

Databases (Core).title: SQLoom: Set-Contrastive Learning of Syntactic, Semantic, and Logical Dependencies for Text-to-SQL
Databases (Core).summary: Text-to-SQL translates natural language questions into SQL queries, enabling database access without writing SQL. Fine-tuning open-weight large language models (LLMs) is cost-effective, but existing methods treat SQL as ordinary text and optimize token-level likelihood without explicitly modeling its syntactic, semantic, and logical requirements. Thus, a single incorrect alias or comparison operator can invalidate a query while contributing little to training loss. We propose SQLoom, a constraint-aware fine-tuning framework with supervision at three levels: syntactic validity under SQL grammar and database schema, semantic alignment between query decisions and the question, and logical consistency across dependent clause decisions. SQLoom extends supervised fine-tuning with a unified set-contrastive objective favoring sets of correct outputs over minimally different incorrect ones at each level. LLM agents propose this supervision, which a SQL parser and execution on counterexample databases verify. We also release Spider-Refined, a training dataset correcting 378 flawed Spider annotations and enriching database schemas. Experiments on Spider, BIRD, and three perturbed Spider variants show that SQLoom improves execution accuracy for Qwen3-1.7B from 62.9% zero-shot to 88.7% on Spider development, reaching 89.2% on Spider test and 73.4% on BIRD development. It outperforms fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and agent-based baselines with up to 70 billion parameters. On question perturbations, SQLoom loses at most 0.6 accuracy points versus up to 12.1 for agent-based methods. It generates SQL in a single pass at 0.42s per query, 23$\times$ faster than a GPT-4-based agent method. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of set-contrastive supervision over token-level training.

Databases (Core).title: EvoOntology: A Self-Evolving Ontology Layer for Data Agents
Databases (Core).summary: Data agents aim to fulfill natural-language instructions over heterogeneous data, including tables, files, and databases. However, data agents face a challenging agent-data gap: heterogeneous data resides outside the agent, while the agent can access it (e.g., column names and file paths) only through generic tools. Existing approaches either let agents directly explore raw data sources or inject manually constructed semantic layers into prompts. However, neither scales well to large heterogeneous data sources nor adapts to different agent behaviors. In this paper, we introduce EvoOntology, a self-evolving ontology layer for data agents. EvoOntology encapsulates the ontology as an MCP server comprising a schema layer, a content layer, and a tool layer, enabling agents to actively query and interact with the ontology at runtime. To this end, we introduce a builder agent for autonomous ontology construction and a self-evolution loop that continuously refines the ontology through attribution-guided typed edits that are accepted only after a backbone-conditional paired evaluation. Experiments on three well-adopted data-agent benchmarks with four LLM backbones demonstrate that EvoOntology consistently outperforms strong baselines and existing semantic-layer approaches, effectively bridging the agent-data gap and enabling more effective interaction with heterogeneous data. Code: https://github.com/ruc-datalab/EvoOntology

Databases (Core).title: Why Tabular Foundation Models Excel on Relational Data They Have Never Seen
Databases (Core).summary: Given a relational database (RDB) storing heterogeneous tabular information, how can we predict missing (or future) values in some target column of interest? As candidate targets are numerous in enterprise settings, it is preferable to avoid learning a new model from scratch each time there is a new prediction task. Frozen foundation models (FMs) based on in-context learning (ICL) and RDB-specific pre-training provide a viable solution, but the ideal design still remains largely unresolved. Perhaps unexpectedly, preliminary evidence has recently shown that existing single-table FMs (aka TFMs), when combined with suitable parameter-free relational encoders, can be quite competitive in practice despite zero exposure to RDB pre-training or relational data of any kind. In this work we first empirically confirm this phenomenon with a more diverse array of experiments. We then turn to our main contribution, namely, surfacing multiple complementary explanations for why TFMs behave so effectively. These explanations ultimately hinge on innate synergies whereby parameter-free encoders map relational effects to fixed-length embeddings that loosely mimic distributions for which TFMs were originally designed; in so doing, desirable single-table properties transfer to relational settings (e.g., convergent posterior predictive distributions). Collectively, our analysis forges new pathways for improving RDB FMs, particularly when we prioritize interpretability and inevitable integration within agentic systems.

Databases (Core).title: SQL-o1: Automatic Text-to-SQL Program Synthesis via Self-Reward Heuristic Search
Databases (Core).summary: Efficient human-database interaction is a core problem in software engineering. Text-to-SQL (Text2SQL) tackles this by mapping natural language questions to executable SQL queries, enabling automatic SQL synthesis and reliable interaction. Although large language models (LLMs) have advanced significantly, current approaches struggle with poor transferability to open-source LLMs, limited robustness against logic and function errors in complex queries, and inefficiencies in structured search. We introduce SQL-o1, a self-reward-driven heuristic search framework built on an agent-based architecture to enhance model reasoning capabilities. SQL-o1 leverages Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for structured, multi-step exploration and incorporates a dynamic pruning strategy to accelerate inference without sacrificing accuracy. On the Spider and BIRD benchmarks, SQL-o1 achieves a 10.8-point execution accuracy improvement on the complex BIRD dataset, surpassing even GPT-4-based models. It exhibits strong few-shot generalization and robust cross-model transferability across open-source LLMs. Our code is available at https://github.com/ShuaiLyu0110/SQL-o1.

Databases (Core).title: Stop Handcrafting Your Engine! GenDB-V: Towards AI-Generated and Formally Verified Database Systems
Databases (Core).summary: For over 50 years, the database community has developed a wide range of successful engines to answer two fundamental questions: how can database systems run faster, and how can we ensure their correctness? Experience with these engines shows that performance depends on hardware and workloads. As both change over time, we repeatedly redesign and rebuild database systems, a time-consuming and expensive process. Correctness remains another long-standing challenge: recent studies continue to uncover wrong-answer bugs even in mature database engines, despite years of development and testing. To address these, we present GenDB-V, a system that enables AI agents to synthesize database engines specialized to hardware and workloads for performance, and formally verified for correctness. GenDB-V supports specialized implementations of SQL templates and general-purpose engines that accept any query within a supported SQL subset. First, we develop SQLSpec to formalize SQL semantics and deterministically construct fixed, implementation-agnostic synthesis targets. Second, we enable joint synthesis of fast code and formal proofs through storage--execution co-optimization, performance-first exploration, and three-layer modular proofs that bridge low-level execution to SQLSpec semantics. Third, we verify the synthesized code and proofs against the fixed synthesis targets in an isolated pipeline, proving SQL correctness and program safety. We evaluate GenDB-V on TPC-H and SEC-EDGAR. For verified template implementations, GenDB-V achieves geometric-mean speedups of 22.0-61.3x over DuckDB and Umbra. For a verified general-purpose engine, GenDB-V also achieves speedups of 1.27-3.4x on TPC-H. GenDB-V also achieves better performance than a testing-based LLM synthesis method, while our audit and tests expose incorrect answers in that method's implementations for 16 of 28 templates.

Databases (Core).title: Recast: Refinement-Centered Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Optimized for Storage
Databases (Core).summary: Large-scale ANNS systems often exploit storage in addition to DRAM for supporting vector search. The central question is how to divide the work between memory and storage for achieving both high query throughput-recall and good index maintenance performance. Existing storage-optimized ANNS paradigms fall short of providing a complete answer: disk-resident graph indexes have difficulty in supporting efficient vector deletions, while posting-list systems often incur more disk I/Os for queries. In this paper, we introduce a refinement-centered paradigm for storage-optimized ANNS systems. We propose Recast as a concrete design of this paradigm. Recast stores raw vectors on disk and keeps an IVF index with our RecastQ quantization encoding in memory. For an ANNS query, Recast selects nprobe inverted lists and performs SIMD-based FastScan on their RecastQ codes to identify refinement candidates in memory. It then retrieves candidate vectors from disk, computes exact distances, and refines the top-K result. To reduce disk I/Os, RecastQ computes uncertainty intervals containing true distances with high probability. Our QUIC policy selects a minimal refinement set based on these intervals, minimizing candidate-retrieval I/Os. Both the on-disk raw vectors and the in-memory IVF structure support insertions and deletions. Experiments on real-world data sets show that Recast processes batched insertions and deletions 3.10-37.27x faster than SPFresh and OdinANN, while its QPS at 0.99 recall changes by at most 6.9% after updating 50% of the corpus. For static queries at 0.99 recall, Recast achieves 1.56-2.01x the QPS of the strongest baseline with the matched memory budget on each data set, while requiring 1.22-6.75x less external storage than the evaluated systems. At matched in-memory space, RecastQ also provides a better Recall-refinement frontier than RaBitQ.

Databases (Core).title: 3L-D: A Low-Light Level Dataset from a Sensor-Agnostic, Alignment-Preserving Acquisition Framework
Databases (Core).summary: Supervised low-light image and video enhancement has achieved remarkable progress, yet current models remain fundamentally constrained by the limitations of existing datasets. Prevailing methods typically rely on uncontrolled ambient captures, camera parameter manipulation (e.g., exposure or ISO adjustments), or neutral density filters, failing to replicate authentic night-sky near-infrared spectral content and genuine low-photon noise distributions. Furthermore, capturing dynamic paired sequences without introducing warping artifacts or sensor-specific biases remains an open challenge. In this paper, we introduce 3L-Dataset, a physically calibrated low-light image and video dataset generated using a modular, sensor-agnostic acquisition framework. Our test bench faithfully reproduces the standardized Midavaine night level scale from Level 1 (full moon, approximately 1000 mlx) down to Level 5 (overcast moonless night, approximately 0.1 mlx), spanning the visible to near-infrared spectrum across diverse realistic environments, including countryside, forest, urban, and desert scale models. Using high-precision programmable mechanical actuation, our acquisition framework guarantees sub-pixel spatial alignment across synchronized sextuplets, each composed of one reference image and five corresponding images acquired at the five standardized night levels, without post-processing image warping. We evaluate multiple representative deep learning baselines across varying night levels, revealing critical trade-offs between reconstruction fidelity, perceptual quality, and inference latency under severe photon starvation. The modular acquisition framework can be adapted to different cameras, optical systems, sensor technologies, and resolutions, enabling the dataset to be continuously expanded.

Databases (Core).title: USDB: Scaling Storage for Next-Generation Recommender Systems at ByteDance
Databases (Core).summary: Recommendation models consume increasingly long, attribute-rich user histories, making small continuous updates and repeated large reads a central storage asymmetry. We present USDB, ByteDance's unified sequence storage practice for streaming and batch workloads. CascadeLSM time-based compaction stages materialize application-specific histories; differentiated replicas share persistent files; partial dumps reconstruct inference inputs from captured recent state and versioned history; and a hybrid columnar format accelerates projected reads. These designs reuse maintenance results across ingestion, inference, and training. Production migration records show 85.8% lower mean write latency, while normalized deployment accounting shows 42.1% lower infrastructure cost. Controlled comparisons with an Optimized RocksDB sequence baseline show faster long-history reads across projections and client loads. Aggregation pushdown sustains 8.5x the throughput of ordinary reads under a constrained receive budget. Production reconstruction and direct-file training results demonstrate how shared sequence maintenance supports fresh serving and repeated historical access.

Databases (Core).title: JetStream: Generating Verified Query Accelerators for Existing Database Systems
Databases (Core).summary: Recent work has shown that LLMs can synthesize highly specialized database systems for fixed workloads, but these systems replace the DBMS's native storage and assume static data: users must migrate their data, often give up ad-hoc queries, and lose acceleration once the data changes. We present JetStream, which instead generates query-specific accelerators that extend an existing DBMS. Given a set of parametrized query templates, a staged agentic workflow synthesizes accelerators that run directly over the DBMS's native tables and may maintain custom auxiliary state, while the DBMS remains responsible for storage, transactions, recovery, and all other queries. A fixed, engine-neutral substrate handles engine-specific hooks and keeps auxiliary state transactionally consistent under writes. JetStream generates two kinds of accelerators: tested accelerators, which may use any optimization and are validated by differential testing, and verified accelerators which trade some performance for a machine-checked proof that every answer satisfies a trusted specification derived from the SQL. On TPC-H at SF=20, JetStream achieves a $315 \times$ geomean read speedup over DuckDB ($93 \times$ verified) and retains $120 \times$ under a continuous update stream of 10,000 modified rows per second.

Databases (Core).title: High-Throughput Private Information Retrieval with on-CPU Accelerators
Databases (Core).summary: Private information retrieval (PIR) hides which record a client retrieves by scanning the entire database, and batching is an effective technique to improve throughput by sharing this scan across queries. However, existing CPU-based solutions gain little from batching because each query still requires its own multiplications, and vector instructions perform only a few at a time. GPUs and other discrete accelerators can accelerate these computations, but require extra hardware and can constrain database size due to their limited memory capacity. In this paper, we present AltoPIR, the first PIR system that leverages on-CPU matrix accelerators such as Intel AMX. AltoPIR keeps the accelerator fed from the CPU caches, reading each database byte from memory once for all queries in a batch and never writing intermediate products to memory. This enables high-performance PIR through efficient batching without requiring discrete accelerators. Our evaluation shows that AltoPIR achieves up to 50.1x higher throughput than existing CPU-based solutions and serves databases larger than a GPU's memory.

Databases (Core).title: Mixed-Type Relational Database Synthesis with Graph-Prompted Language Model
Databases (Core).summary: Data access is often limited by privacy or proprietary restrictions, motivating relational database synthesis, which synthesizes realistic contents across related tables. Relational databases couple multi-table structure with mixed-type attributes and intricate semantic dependencies among values, making realistic synthesis challenging. In this paper, we propose REMIX, a unified framework for realistic relational database synthesis with mixed-type attributes. REMIX integrates a small language model (SLM) and a large language model (LLM) through two key phases: Graph-to-Prompt Tuning and Collaborative SLM-LLM Decoding. To capture attribute dependencies within and across tables, Graph-to-Prompt Tuning represents the database as an attributed heterogeneous graph. We project mixed-type record embeddings and aggregated relational context into soft prompts that serve as continuous vectors for an SLM. We jointly optimize the graph-to-prompt mapping and SLM through autoregressive attribute reconstruction. Furthermore, to reduce semantic inconsistencies, Collaborative SLM-LLM Decoding combines SLM-based record generation with repair programs induced by an LLM. The LLM discovers semantic dependencies, iteratively refines them through independent validation with a statistical bound on the overall probability of false acceptance, and translates validated dependencies into tested programs that repair generated values. Extensive experiments on seven real-world relational databases demonstrate the effectiveness of REMIX in generating high-fidelity data with improved semantic consistency and downstream utility.

Databases (Core).title: Complexity of conjunctive regular path query homomorphisms
Databases (Core).summary:
A graph database is a digraph whose arcs are labeled with symbols from a fixed alphabet. A regular graph pattern (RGP) is a digraph whose arcs are labeled with regular expressions over the alphabet. RGPs model navigational queries for graph databases called \emph{conjunctive regular path queries} (CRPQs). A match of a CRPQ in the database is witnessed by a special navigational homomorphism of the corresponding RGP to the database, where vertices of the RGP are mapped by a function $f$ to the vertices of the database, and for each arc $uv$ of the RGP, we require the existence of a walk in the database from $f(u)$ to $f(v)$, such that the word corresponding to the sequence of labels of that walk belongs to the regular language labeling the arc $uv$.
  We extend this definition to one of navigational homomorphisms between two RGPs, modeling a homomorphism-based form of CRPQ containment. We study the complexity of deciding the existence of such a homomorphism between RGPs. We show that this problem, in the case where general walks are considered, can still be solved by an EXPSPACE algorithm (just like general CRPQ Containment, which is known to be EXPSPACE-complete). In the case of simple paths or trails, in fact the navigational homomorphism problem considered here becomes much more tractable, as it is PSPACE-complete. We also study the problem for restricted RGPs over a unary alphabet, that arise from some applications like XPath or SPARQL. For this case, homomorphism-based CRPQ containment is in NP. We prove that certain interesting cases are in fact polynomial-time solvable.
Databases (Core).comment: 24 pages, 7 figures. A short version appeared in the proceedings of the 15th Conference on Computability in Europe (CIE 2019). This improved version corrects mistakes from earlier versions, contains new results, and has one additional author

Databases (Core).title: FPT iff PTIME for Homomorphism Problems on Sparse-Incidence and Bounded-Independence Patterns
Databases (Core).summary:
We show that fixed-parameter tractability and polynomial-time solvability coincide for homomorphism problems specified by classes of pattern hypergraphs of bounded incidence degeneracy or bounded primal independence number, assuming $FPT 
e W[1]$. In both cases, tractability is characterised by bounded fractional hypertree width. This generalises a result of Grohe [JACM 2007] that established such an FPT-PTIME collapse for bounded-arity structures. We build on the fractional balanced-separator framework and rounding theorem of Korchemna, Lokshtanov, Saurabh, Surianarayanan, and Xue [FOCS 2024] to prove near-linear bounds on fractional hypertree width ($fhw$) in terms of adaptive width ($adw$). Namely, for every hypergraph $H$ $$fhw(H)=O(μ(H) adw(H)\log adw(H)), \quad fhw(H)=O(\log α(H) adw(H)\log adw(H))$$ where $μ(H)$ is the degeneracy of the incidence graph of $H$ and $α(H)$ the independence number of the primal graph of $H$. As a consequence, we obtain a corresponding FPT-PTIME collapse for exact homomorphism decision and counting on every class in which either incidence degeneracy or independence number is bounded. This includes a number of natural classes such as pattern hypergraphs of bounded degree. Additionally, we observe that for every r.e. class of pattern hypergraphs, fixed-parameter tractability of the parameterised homomorphism problem implies quasipolynomial-time solvability of the corresponding unparameterised problem, assuming $FPT 
e W[1]$. Our results rely on the characterisation of fixed-parameter tractable decision of homomorphism problems in terms of submodular width of Marx [JACM 2013], conditional on ETH. In light of the very recent potential refutation of the ETH, we show that the characterisation of Marx holds also under the assumption that $FPT 
e W[1]$.

Databases (Core).title: Modular and Efficient Approximate Nearest Neighbors Search with Vectorium and kANNolo
Databases (Core).summary: Approximate Nearest Neighbors (ANN) search over neural embeddings powers modern retrieval systems such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Embeddings come in three representations (dense, sparse and multi-vector), and efficient search combines an index structure, a similarity function and a quantization scheme. Existing libraries fix one combination, hard-code each one separately, or factor only one side of the problem, and none covers all three representations. We present Vectorium and kANNolo, two open-source Rust libraries that split this design space into a data-management layer and an indexing layer. Vectorium abstracts the vector, the distance function, the quantizer and the dataset independently, and provides 11 encoders, from 32-bit floats to sub-bit codes. On top of it, kANNolo implements Hierarchical Navigable Small-World (HNSW) graph and Inverted Vector File (IVF) indexes that are generic over representation, encoder and metric, and a two-stage index that composes any first-stage index with any rescoring dataset. Since every combination is specialized at compile time, this modularity adds no run-time overhead, and the resulting indexes reach state-of-the-art performance: our Product Quantization matches Faiss in accuracy at competitive speed, our RaBitQ and HNSW match or outperform their reference implementations, and our IVF outperforms Faiss. Against six dense and five sparse systems on seven public collections, our indexes give the best memory-throughput trade-off on dense data in 9 of 12 collection-accuracy pairs and perform well on out-of-distribution queries. On sparse data, the systems built on Vectorium lead on all three collections, with Seismic and SeismicWave the fastest and kANNolo's indexes the most compact.
Databases (Core).comment: 39 pages, 11 figures, 17 tables. Submitted to Information Systems. Code and data: https://github.com/TusKANNy/papers_reproducibility/tree/main/information-systems-vectorium-kannolo

Databases (Core).title: Teach Your DBMS to LIKE Strings: Fast and General Pattern Matching for Wildcard Joins and Filters
Databases (Core).summary: Nowadays, modern applications do more than just store text -- they need to derive meaningful insights from it. To do that, they usually rely on wildcard queries with LIKE predicate to extract patterns. However, modern database management systems (DBMSs) handle these wildcard operations poorly, resorting to nested loops for joins and expensive interpreted evaluation for filters. To address the former, we propose a new join algorithm based on the Aho-Corasick algorithm, which significantly reduces the time complexity. For wildcard filtering, we leverage the code-generation infrastructure to improve performance: we generate specialized code for the LIKE predicate, eliminating the overhead of interpreting the pattern per tuple. Our experimental results show that the new wildcard join algorithm significantly outperforms both baseline DuckDB and Umbra, achieving speedups of up to 30.6x and 114.75x, respectively. The new wildcard filter approach likewise outperforms both baselines, achieving a speedup of 13.3x in a filter-focused stress benchmark. We believe these two techniques will play key roles for high-performance text analytics in modern query engines.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: Strategist: Evolving Reasoning with Agents
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: A model is only half of an AI agent system. The other half is the inference strategy: the reasoning procedure that turns model calls into a response. Today that second half is written by hand, and the experience of building one strategy never carries to the next. We introduce Strategist, a meta-agent that evolves inference strategies across tasks. Each strategy is written as a blueprint,executable code that other strategies can reuse, and together the blueprints form a library. Given a task and a small development set, Strategist retrieves related blueprints, writes candidate strategies, tests them on real samples, and revises them from the results. Every candidate then enters the library, so later tasks build on earlier discoveries. On 30 benchmarks, Strategist beats the strongest baseline on 24 and matches its average accuracy (74.7% vs.74.0%) at 39% lower inference cost. Its strategies also transfer to unseen tasks and other models without further search. The part of an AI system that is not improved on its own now does.
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.comment: NeurIPS 2026

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: CoSpaDi: Compressing LLMs via Calibration-Guided Sparse Dictionary Learning
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Post-training LLM compression often relies on low-rank approximations, which force all columns of a projection matrix to share a single low-dimensional subspace. We propose CoSpaDi, a training-free compression framework that replaces this single-subspace assumption with a union-of-subspaces model via sparse dictionary learning. CoSpaDi factorizes each weight matrix into a dense dictionary and column-sparse coefficients, allowing different columns to select different subsets of dictionary atoms at the same storage budget. To preserve model behavior, we use calibration activations to transform functional reconstruction into a standard dictionary learning problem. Across LLaMA and Qwen models, CoSpaDi improves accuracy-compression and perplexity-compression trade-offs over SVD-based and structured pruning baselines at 20-40\% compression ratios, while naturally supporting sparse-dense computation and post-training quantization of sparse coefficients.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: Evaluating Uncertainty Calibration in Probabilistic Time Series Foundation Models
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are increasingly used for probabilistic forecasting across diverse domains, yet the reliability of their uncertainty estimates remains poorly understood. In this work, we study uncertainty calibration in probabilistic TSFMs from a broader methodological and empirical perspective. We introduce a taxonomy of how TSFMs represent predictive uncertainty and develop a fine-grained evaluation framework for calibration in multi-horizon forecasting that distinguishes pooled, horizon-wise, and stronger conditional notions of calibration. Using this framework, we conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation of popular TSFMs across diverse datasets and show that current models exhibit distinct and systematic patterns of miscalibration that standard metrics often obscure. We further analyze common post-hoc recalibration methods and characterize which forms of calibration they can improve and which tend to persist. Our results provide practical guidance for evaluating and improving uncertainty calibration in TSFMs and highlight important limitations of current practice.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: Can We Stop the Backtest Yet? Anytime-Valid Promotion Tests for Adaptive Financial Research Agents
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Financial research agents can generate and monitor trading rules faster than a human can document the resulting selection process. Candidates appear at data-dependent times, weak rules are abandoned, and promising ones are watched until they cross a reporting threshold. We introduce PROMOTE, a protocol that assigns every candidate predictable testing wealth at birth and accumulates a cost-aware e-process only from subsequent returns. If lifetime allocations sum to at most one, a weighted Ville argument bounds the probability of ever promoting a rule whose declared bounded net score has always had nonpositive conditional mean. The result permits dependent candidates, adaptive births, and indefinite monitoring. We audit the implementation in two settings. A retrospective pseudo-out-of-sample replay contains 24 panel--rule hypotheses, 3,000 shared-sign null paths, injected alternatives, and public ETF and industry data. Repeated unadjusted tests produce a family crossing in 94.5% of null paths, versus 0.0% for PROMOTE; at a 15-bp aligned ETF-component perturbation, PROMOTE has 70.1% target power and median crossing session 2,327. A separate exact mean-zero experiment lets an agent select candidate identities and birth times from past scores; the funded gate has 1.77% false-family crossings across 3,000 programs. The market replay produces zero promotions after costs. The certificate controls historical false promotion under the declared null; it is not a certificate that an earlier edge remains profitable at deployment. AI-use disclosure. Generative AI tools, including OpenAI Codex, assisted manuscript preparation. For this preprint version, Codex assisted with LaTeX editing, author and venue metadata, compilation, and layout checks.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: TRACER: Token ReAssignment for Concept ERasure in Generative Recommendation
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary:
Generative recommendation formulates next-item prediction as autoregressive generation over semantic ID (SID) sequences derived from users' historical interactions, making modern recommender systems structurally similar to large language models (LLMs). As privacy and safety concerns grow, these systems increasingly require concept unlearning to remove sensitive or harmful concepts associated with items. However, existing LLM unlearning methods cannot be directly applied to generative recommendation. Unlike word tokens with explicit semantics, SIDs are abstract identifiers that are often shared by both forget and retain items, leading to severe conflicts between concept removal and recommendation utility preservation.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Testable and Actionable Calibration for Full Swap Regret
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: AI generated predictions increasingly inform decision making in critical tasks, and therefore must be trustworthy. One widely used measure of trustworthiness is calibration, which requires that the predictions match the true frequencies and can be treated like real probabilities of a given outcome. However, defining calibration is subtle, and designing good measures of calibration error has been an active topic of recent research. The first goal is to find calibration measures that are actionable, meaning they can inform decision makers about their utility loss when predictions are treated as true probabilities, which is known as swap regret. The second goal is to find calibration measures that are testable, meaning that calibration error can be measured from a small sample of predictions and outcomes. Although these are very basic requirements, there is no existing calibration measure that fully satisfies both properties, and all existing measures relax actionability by bounding a weaker notion of swap regret, or relax testability by having suboptimal estimation error. We introduce a new calibration measure, Soft-Binned Calibration Decision Loss (SCDL), which we prove is fully actionable without weakening either requirement, and testable with nearly optimal error rate. In addition, SCDL satisfies other desired properties such as continuity and consistency. We also provide a set of experiments confirming that the theoretical advantages of SCDL compared to other measures lead to better performance in practice.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Unrolled gradients in disguise: bridging interpolation-based and Jacobian regularization for stable neural dynamics
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Hybrid models and neural differential equations (NDEs) are becoming increasingly important for modelling physical systems; however, they often encounter stability and accuracy issues during long-term integration. In this work, we demonstrate that these paradigms can be understood under a common lens and that they both correspond to an approximation of the gradients obtained in an unrolled learning strategy. Building on this understanding, we derive a principled and complete approach to regularize training and demonstrate its impact on the stability of learned dynamical systems.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Online Class Posteriors for Interpretable and Controllable Discrete Diffusion

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Subpolynomial-Query Proximal Sampling Beyond Log-Concavity
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: We study the gradient query complexity of sampling from a density $π(x)\propto\mathrm{e}^{-V(x)}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $V$ has a $β$-Lipschitz gradient but need not be convex. Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: TRACER: Token ReAssignment for Concept ERasure in Generative Recommendation
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary:
Generative recommendation formulates next-item prediction as autoregressive generation over semantic ID (SID) sequences derived from users' historical interactions, making modern recommender systems structurally similar to large language models (LLMs). As privacy and safety concerns grow, these systems increasingly require concept unlearning to remove sensitive or harmful concepts associated with items. However, existing LLM unlearning methods cannot be directly applied to generative recommendation. Unlike word tokens with explicit semantics, SIDs are abstract identifiers that are often shared by both forget and retain items, leading to severe conflicts between concept removal and recommendation utility preservation.

Rather than directly suppressing shared SIDs, TRACER reassigns concept-related items to alternative tokens that better facilitate forgetting while minimizing side effects on retained items. We further introduce a coherence regularizer to preserve semantic consistency among retain items during unlearning. Experiments on real-world recommendation datasets demonstrate that TRACER effectively removes target concepts while substantially better preserving recommendation utility than existing unlearning baselines.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: ENGINE: Endogenous Variational MultiScale Optimization for Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient large language model (LLM) fine-tuning, and recent methods incorporate curvature-aware strategies. However, in the high-dimensional parameter space of LLMs, these methods inherently suffer from exploding gradient variance and prohibitive costs. Conversely, confining updates to a low-dimensional subspace reduces variance but discards critical high-dimensional information, degrading performance. This creates a fundamental dilemma: full-space optimization is informative but has high variance, while subspace optimization has low variance but loses information. To break this trade-off, we propose ENGINE (Endogenous Variational MultiScale). Inspired by computational mechanics, we adapt static Variational MultiScale (VMS) theory to dynamic optimization, treating low- and high-dimensional spaces as resolved coarse and unresolved fine scales. Through a multigrid-style V-cycle, ENGINE alternates between spaces, dynamically probing fine-grained information in the high-dimensional space and injecting it to correct the efficient low-dimensional sampling process. Under appropriate assumptions, statistical analysis characterizes variance reduction and correction of curvature-induced bias, and convergence analysis establishes a stationarity bound for the corrected coarse updates. Evaluations on standard LLM benchmarks show that ENGINE achieves higher accuracy and faster convergence than existing ZO methods, achieving up to a $2.61\times$ speed-up in forward passes with zero additional peak memory overhead. Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Quantizing With Randomized Hadamard Transforms: Efficient Heuristic Now Proven
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Uniform random rotations (URRs) are a common preprocessing step in modern quantization approaches used for gradient compression, inference acceleration, KV-cache compression, model weight quantization, and approximate nearest-neighbor search in vector databases. The remaining issue is the performance for worst-case inputs. With a URR, each coordinate is distributed as a shifted beta distribution, which converges to a Gaussian distribution in high dimensions. Generally, one RHT is not suitable in the worst case, as individual coordinates can be far from these distributions. We show that after composing two RHTs on any $d$-sized input vector, the marginal distribution of every fixed coordinate of the normalized rotated vector is within $O(d^{-1/2})$ of a standard Gaussian both in Kolmogorov distance and in $1$-Wasserstein distance. We then plug these bounds into the analyses of modern compression schemes, namely DRIVE and QUIC-FL, and show that two RHTs achieve performance that asymptotically matches URRs. However, while two RHTs suffice for scalar quantization, they may be insufficient for Vector Quantization (VQ), which depends on the joint distribution across fixed-size blocks of coordinates (as opposed to only marginal distribution convergence for single coordinates). We prove that a composition of three RHTs leads to decaying coordinate covariance. This ensures that any fixed, bounded, multi-dimensional VQ codebook optimized for URRs has the same expected error when using three RHTs, up to an additive term that vanishes with the dimension. Finally, because practical inputs are rarely adversarial, we propose a linear-time $O(d)$ check on the input's moments to dynamically adapt the number of RHTs used at runtime to improve performance.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: A Witnessing Duality for ReLU Network Depth

Biases may be arbitrary rationals. The refuter finds a rational input on which the network fails, and its correctness is provable in $\mathbf{VTC}^0$, the bounded-arithmetic theory of uniform constant-depth threshold computation. The underlying numerical depth lower bound follows from Averkov, Hojny and Merkert (ICLR 2025), extending Haase, Hertrich and Loho (ICLR 2023); our contribution is an internal proof that makes its geometric argument into a feasible refuter. On the construction side, $\mathbf{VTC}^0$ verifies locally checkable certificates for the balanced integer-weight maximum network of depth $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$. At $q=2$, the construction and refuter meet: for each fixed $K$, the theory verifies that integer-nonbias-weight networks with arbitrary rational biases can compute the maximum with at most $K$ hidden layers exactly when $n\le 2^K$. We also give certified rational constructions of polynomial encoding length and depth $O(\log n/\log\log n)$. Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Causal discovery needs explicit epistemic standards
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: There are many causal discovery algorithms, but few guiding principles for choosing between them. Methods are usually compared through three lenses: identifiability, consistency, and benchmarks. Each introduces assumptions about the data-generating process that are often untestable. We argue that there are no shared standards for comparing, prioritizing, or even discussing those assumptions. We support this claim by showing that (i) identifiability assumptions are often preferred by convention rather than by principle, (ii) uniform consistency requires further untestable assumptions, while the weaker pointwise consistency has arguably narrowed algorithm design, and (iii) benchmarks are not neutral tests but carry an epistemic role of their own: they quietly fix which regimes matter, which guarantees come into play, and what counts as success. In doing so, they shape what algorithm comparisons are taken to show and thus perform some of the same epistemic work as theory, but less transparently. In this position paper we argue for a more transparent, integrated practice: Make the epistemic standards for discussing identifiability and consistency assumptions explicit, especially their failure modes and scope conditions; design benchmarks to operationalize those standards, by stress-testing and ablating both. Then, theoretical and empirical results jointly clarify when, why, and how algorithms may work rather than accumulate as disconnected advances.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Optimal Subgroup Discovery at Every Support Threshold
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Subgroup discovery aims to identify regions of the feature space where a target variable deviates from its marginal distribution. Existing methods tackle this challenge by collapsing the two into a single scalar quality measure, implicitly committing to one particular trade-off and making it difficult to recover the most deviating subgroup under a user-specified support constraint. Under a partition-based generative model, where the feature space decomposes into regions of homogeneous conditional distributions of the target variable called atoms, we prove that every point on the deviation-support Pareto front is a union of whole atoms together with at most one fractional atom. This reduces an uncountable search to a finite combinatorial problem. Guided by this theory, we propose a simple two-step recipe: learn a homogeneous partition, then select atoms greedily. Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Dense Structural Compression of Transformers via Gauge-Correct Channel Removal
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary:
Inference energy per token drives the cost and carbon footprint of deployed transformers. It is dominated by dense matrix products that incur fused multiply-accumulate (FMA) operations and memory traffic. To reduce these computations while retaining dense tensors for high GPU throughput, we develop a methodology from first principles to adapt structural complexity during training to maximize inference utility per unit compute. Channel penalties drive entire tensor slices to zero to enable physical removal while preserving density and the network function.
  The natural approach, penalizing the norm of operator components acting through each channel, is provably destabilized by gauge freedom. We resolve this pathology with GaugeLasso: additive symmetric group-lasso penalties that recover a monotone function of product-norms when the network converges to gauge balance. Our equilibrium analysis enables per-channel calibration to correctly suppress slices that under-perform in inference utility per unit compute.
  Under adaptive pressure, the network reorganizes into depth-dependent structural profiles that can be far smaller than the architecture required to learn the task. On polynomial long division over $\mathbb{F}_{31}$, compute compresses from 148 to 255 times with perfect accuracy. On character-level language modeling, compressed models outperform the hand-designed baseline at equal FMA. On masked autoencoding, a compression trial exposes which axes were over-provisioned and which saturated, guiding a better second design. Compaction also accelerates training monotonically as the model progresses. Post-hoc pruning with the same utility ranking cannot reach these structures, showing that sustained pressure is central to discovery of efficient models. Retraining a discovered architecture recovers baseline quality on our statistical tasks, but fails on our exact algorithmic task.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Dynamic regret measures an online learner against a moving comparator, and standard analyses assume the learner may move freely at every round. On a domain of diameter $D$ with $G$-Lipschitz convex losses, for every comparator path length $P_T \in [D, DT]$ we exhibit a deterministic adversary that forces $R_d = Ω(GDT)$ on every budget-feasible algorithm whenever $S \le c P_T$ for a universal constant $c>0$. Conversely, projected online gradient descent with a budget-aware step size is budget-feasible and attains $o(GDT)$ once $S = ω(D + P_T)$. Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: LEAD: Length-Efficient Adaptive and Dynamic Reasoning for Large Language Models

Furthermore, it estimates an adaptive per-problem target length online based on the model's own correct rollouts, applying a symmetric efficiency reward that penalizes both overthinking and over-compression. Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Sparse attention cuts the cost of long-context inference by making the attention matrix sparse: each query attends only a subset of the sequence, chosen by a fixed pattern or, in recent production LLMs, learned per query. In DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), the attention of DeepSeek-V3.2 and the GLM-5 family, every layer is preceded by a lightning indexer that scores the whole cache and keeps the k=2048 highest-scoring tokens for the layer to attend. At long context this indexer scan, not the sparse attention it feeds, is where the decode time goes. But adjacent layers select nearly the same tokens, so a layer can attend the selection of the previous indexer layer instead of its own. This removes the dependency: each indexer then runs concurrently with the attention of its layer. The resulting Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) needs no retraining and no new weights. Its default realization changes no kernel, running inside SGLang's production decode graph; an optional fused decode kernel accelerates it further on DeepSeek-V3.2. MLI composes with IndexCache (the cross-layer reuse GLM-5.2 ships as IndexShare): IndexCache drops the indexer from some layers, and MLI hides the scan on the rest. At equal retention the composition decodes faster than IndexCache: up to 14.5% faster on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at 1/2, and 7.9% and 5.1% at 1/4, largest where IndexCache keeps the most indexers and growing with context. At retention 1/r it is faster still than IndexCache at 1/(2r) while keeping twice the fresh selections: at 128K it reaches 1.32x the unmodified model's decode throughput at 1/4, above IndexCache's 1.28x at 1/8. NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Strategist: Evolving Reasoning with Agents
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: A model is only half of an AI agent system. The other half is the inference strategy: the reasoning procedure that turns model calls into a response. NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: CoSpaDi: Compressing LLMs via Calibration-Guided Sparse Dictionary Learning

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: TRACER: Token ReAssignment for Concept ERasure in Generative Recommendation
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary:
Generative recommendation formulates next-item prediction as autoregressive generation over semantic ID (SID) sequences derived from users' historical interactions, making modern recommender systems structurally similar to large language models (LLMs). As privacy and safety concerns grow, these systems increasingly require concept unlearning to remove sensitive or harmful concepts associated with items. However, existing LLM unlearning methods cannot be directly applied to generative recommendation. Unlike word tokens with explicit semantics, SIDs are abstract identifiers that are often shared by both forget and retain items, leading to severe conflicts between concept removal and recommendation utility preservation.

Rather than directly suppressing shared SIDs, TRACER reassigns concept-related items to alternative tokens that better facilitate forgetting while minimizing side effects on retained items. We further introduce a coherence regularizer to preserve semantic consistency among retain items during unlearning. Experiments on real-world recommendation datasets demonstrate that TRACER effectively removes target concepts while substantially better preserving recommendation utility than existing unlearning baselines.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: EntropyCache: Decoded Token Entropy Guided KV Caching for Diffusion Language Models

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: SLATE: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Long-Horizon API Selection in E-commerce Tool Use
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Enterprises increasingly want LLM agents to automate standard operating procedures over their software stacks -- mapping each step of a procedure to the right call among thousands of internal APIs, without hand-authored step-to-API mappings. The core difficulty is API selection at scale: choosing and composing the correct tools over a long horizon, judged only by whether the overall task succeeds. Current tool-use benchmarks do not test this regime -- they expose only a handful of tools, evaluate single-step invocation, or grade multi-step behavior with subjective LLM-as-a-judge scores that penalize valid alternative trajectories. We introduce SLATE (Synthetic Large-scale API Toolkit for E-commerce), a large-scale benchmark that tests large-toolset, long-horizon API selection in a realistic enterprise domain. SLATE couples (i) queries decomposed into hierarchical, tool-grounded procedures over a ~1,000-tool e-commerce library, (ii) a deterministic, context-aware simulator that returns recorded outputs for matching calls and default responses otherwise, and (iii) an end-to-end task-success metric -- a task succeeds when it reaches every reference outcome -- that credits diverse-but-valid trajectories while remaining fully automatic and reproducible. Experiments with six open decision models and the language models they are built on, from 3B to 12B parameters, show that even the best model completes only 5.0% of the tasks, establishing SLATE as a challenging testbed for reliable enterprise tool use. We release SLATE, its simulator, and the evaluation harness at https://geshijoker.github.io/slate/

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: From Senses to Decisions: The Information Flow of Auditory and Visual Perception in Multimodal LLMs
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can listen and see, but how do audio and visual signals actually travel through the network to shape an answer? Despite their growing role in research and real-world applications, the internal pathways through which audio and visual tokens influence the final prediction remain poorly understood. In this study, we examine audio-visual information flow inside Audio-Visual Large Language Models (AVLLMs), tracing how AVLLMs route, utilize, and integrate audio and visual information across two input configurations, audio-visual video and multiple interleaved audio-visual items. We find that for audio-visual video, AVLLMs follow the sequential information flow pathway established for VLMs and VideoLLMs, with audio and visual contribution flowing along this pathway in proportion to the task's reliance on each modality. In settings with multiple interleaved audio-visual items, this routing shifts to different parallel streams. Furthermore, we demonstrate that audio-visual and other token types can be discarded once their information is transferred to LLM, with minimal impact on the model's prediction or even slight improvement, generalizing across multiple tasks and datasets, enabling more efficient inference. These findings hold across multiple models and scales, Qwen2.5-Omni and Video-SALMONN2 Plus at 3B and 7B scales, leading to hypotheses on why these flow structures emerge. Together, these results deliver the first coherent picture of how AVLLMs orchestrate sound and sight inside the network and lay the groundwork for the next wave of interpretability, design, and efficiency advances in audio-visual and broader MLLMs.
